extracted.intended_audience: reviewers and authors for ACL'23 (especially novice reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical tutorial and policy-oriented guidance for reviewing and responding to submissions to ACL'23, covering reviewer qualifications, conflicts, reading strategy, writing reviews, discussion, and author rebuttal behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of submissions and reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: All the information about submissions and reviews that you receive as part of your assignment is confidential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you participate in discussions of peer review on social media, make sure your comments/examples are general enough that no submissions can be identified, and the authors cannot identify you. Do not refer to individual papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain accurate reviewer profile for matching
rubrics_metrics.description: Check that you have provided all the information about you, which the venue asked for - any sign-up forms, reviewer profiles etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is used for computing conflicts of interest and paper-reviewer assignments. For ACL 2023, ensure your Semantic Scholar/global profile is accurate so you are more likely to get papers in your area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess whether you are qualified to review
rubrics_metrics.description: As soon as you get an assignment, skim the paper to check whether this is something that you are qualified to review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is acceptable to be asked to review slightly outside your subfield if you know the core methodology; if your expertise does not cover certain aspects, your review should specify that. Note upsides of imperfect matches (learning, cross-field feedback).

rubrics_metrics.name: Declare conflicts of interest and preserve anonymization
rubrics_metrics.description: If the venue implements a fully or partially anonymous review process, check whether you know or can guess who the authors are and whether anonymity is preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If anonymity is not preserved, contact your chair/action editor and the paper should be desk-rejected. If you know the authors from personal contact, ask for re-assignment or indicate awareness of authors’ identity in the review form. For academic conflicts (very close to your own work), recuse and contact senior area chair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desk-reject criteria (anonymity/style/page limit violations)
rubrics_metrics.description: You can indicate that the paper should be desk-rejected if it does not follow the style guides or goes over the page limit (which does not include the ethical considerations section).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact your chair or action editor about desk-rejection; note that anonymity violations are grounds for desk-reject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan and manage review time
rubrics_metrics.description: When you accept an assignment, please block the time in your calendar for working on that review and submitting it on time, preferably at least a few days before the deadline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate time needed for reading and writing; avoid reviewing in a single session—write a first draft and revisit later to reduce knee-jerk reactions. Submitting early gives AC/AEs time to catch grave issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid commenting during first read; use staged reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid commenting during the very first read. First skim to understand the overall type of contribution and framework; then read introduction and methodology carefully before looking at results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For experimental papers, do not look at results on first skim. After reading intro/methods, ask: is the research question clear? Would the methods answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Only then examine results—this helps judge the knowledge gained, even if results are negative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge the paper for what it is (paper-type appropriate evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any study should be judged for what it is, and not for what you think it should be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of different contribution types (resource papers, model/linguistic analysis, data processing/annotation, reproduction, surveys, position pieces, negative results) and evaluate according to expectations for that type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust expectations by paper length
rubrics_metrics.description: Note whether the paper is long or short, and adjust your expectations accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long papers should describe completed work with thorough evaluation/analysis. Short papers may present proof of concept or an interesting finding and are not expected to have extensive evaluation—only the minimal but sufficiently convincing evidence for the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious looking up references to avoid de-anonymization
rubrics_metrics.description: While you read, you may want to look up some references or concurrent work. This should be done cautiously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many papers have non-anonymous preprints, and looking up references may accidentally reveal authors’ identities, opening you to social biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write reviews with multiple audiences in mind
rubrics_metrics.description: A review is read by authors, other reviewers, the area chair (AC), and the senior area chair (SAC); consider them when writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For authors: be respectful and thorough and give a clear path forward (actionable suggestions). For other reviewers: open doors for discussion. For AC/SAC: make reviews as specific and self-contained as possible because they may not read the paper as closely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide actionable, specific feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should have a clear path forward on how to improve the paper; vague remarks are unhelpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of 'not enough experiments' provide concrete suggestions (e.g., 'the results would be stronger with validation on the LDC NYT dataset'). When new issues arise in discussion, edit your review so authors see relevant information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicate reviewer confidence and expertise limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: If your expertise does not cover certain aspects of the submission, your review should specify that, and most NLP venues let you indicate your confidence score in the review form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state which parts you are less confident about; use the confidence score to help ACs weigh comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author response purpose and constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary purpose of the author response period is to make sure that the reviewers understand the paper correctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reviewer misunderstood claims, the authors should point to where the claims are stated. If requested changes are easy and camera-ready appropriate, authors should state how they'll address them. ACL'23 disallows reporting new experimental results performed after submission; consider whether such results are necessary to back up the claims (if so, missing results are a weakness; otherwise they are suggestions). Flag review policy violations in rebuttal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Update reviews when new information appears
rubrics_metrics.description: If something new comes to light, make sure to modify your review so that the authors have all of the relevant information to revise their paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors will only see the final review text, not necessarily the discussion; incorporate important discussion points into your review text when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participate in post-review discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: After the author responses are in, the area chair may invite reviewers to discuss the paper; please participate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussion helps catch mistakes, misunderstandings, and policy violations and is an opportunity to exchange opinions—this benefits both reviewers and authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of and mitigate implicit biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit biases due to social and academic backgrounds can affect evaluation (e.g., task popularity, language, engineering vs linguistic focus, preprints, famous labs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge that biases are often unconscious; actively consider whether your judgments are influenced by such factors and focus on the paper's merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recuse when submission is too close to your own work
rubrics_metrics.description: If the submission looks like something that is very close to your own work about to be submitted, it is best to recuse yourself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact your senior area chair to recuse; better to avoid reviewing very-close competitors to preserve fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use professional, constructive tone and engage respectfully
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews should be professional and constructive; when disagreeing with other reviewers you may say 'unlike Reviewer 2, I ...' but remember to be professional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid harsh language; helpful resources on avoiding harsh language and responsible reviewing are linked in the tutorial.
